This is the last step of a project: taking your results home from Statistics
Denmark (DST), which DST calls *hjemtagelse* (repatriation). Read it before you
build the tables and figures you plan to export ([Phase 13](analysis.qmd)), and
use the checklist at the bottom before you upload. The data on the research
machine are microdata: they stay there, and results leave only through DST's
repatriation tool, after you have checked them against DST's rules.

::: {.callout-important}
**This page is an overview. DST's own rules take precedence, and they can
change: read them before you export.**

- [DST: Rules for repatriation of analysis results (in
  Danish)](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/regler-og-datasikkerhed/regler-for-hjemtagelse-af-analyseresultater)
- [DST: guidance on the data security rules, with worked examples (PDF, in
  Danish, April
  2024)](https://www.dst.dk/ext/158751994932/0/forskning/Vejledning-i-datasikkerhedsreglerne-under-Mikrodataordningerne-herunder-for-hjemsendelse-af-analyseresultater-og-sanktioner-ved-databru--pdf)

The Danish quotes on this page are from those two sources.
:::

## What may leave DST?

DST lets you take analysis results and other material home when three
conditions all hold: nothing at the level of individuals (or their
pseudonymised keys) is left in it, it is aggregated enough that no person can be
identified or recognised "hverken direkte eller indirekte" (neither directly
nor indirectly), and the file is of an approved type and goes through the
repatriation tool.

What can meet those conditions:

- Aggregated tables
- Figures built from aggregated numbers (see [figures](#figures-and-curves)
  below)
- Analysis results, such as model estimates with confidence intervals
- Scripts. Program code is an approved file type and goes through the same
  tool. It must not contain microdata either: DST's guidance (page 10) names
  code with microdata written into a condition, such as a `pnr` value in a
  filter, and log files that list observations.

What never leaves:

- Individual-level data in any form, also with `pnr` removed
- Small cells, see the threshold below
- Results that could identify a person, directly or indirectly
- Copied notes, screenshots or photographs of the screen. DST's rule names
  them: no microdata may be taken home by copying information down, or by
  "et skærmprint eller et billede af skærmen med din mobiltelefon" (a
  screenshot or a picture of the screen with your phone). See also [DST's rules for working with
  microdata](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/regler-og-datasikkerhed/regler-for-arbejdet-med-mikrodata).

## Which cell size applies to you

DST's baseline is at least 3 observations per table cell. Some registers are
stricter:

> "Der skal være mindst 3 observationer pr. tabelcelle [...]. For enkelte
> registre kan der være strengere krav, for eksempel mindst 5 observationer pr.
> tabelcelle. Hvis dette er tilfældet, vil det fremgå i DDV App, når du
> bestiller data."

In English: at least 3 observations per table cell; for some registers the
requirement can be stricter, for example at least 5; if so, it is shown in DDV
App (DDV is Danmarks Datavindue at DST) when you order the data. Check there which rule applies to your project.

The rule applies at the finest level of the table: if you cross two variables,
every cell of the cross-tabulation must hold the minimum. DST also says the
number is a guide and the responsibility is yours: if you doubt that 3 (or 5)
is enough to keep people anonymous, aggregate further.

This page uses 5 throughout, because it is the safe side of both rules. If your project
is on the baseline of 3, nothing here breaks: you are reporting more
conservatively than required.

## A hidden number must not be possible to work out {#back-calculation}

Hiding the small cells is not enough on its own. DST's rules also say that a
hidden number must not be possible to work out again from the rest of what you
take home:

> "Observationer, som er blevet aggregeret eller på anden vis sløret eller
> fjernet i en tabel, graf eller figur, må ikke kunne udledes ved tilbageregning
> eller krydslæsning. Hvis dette er muligt, skal der aggregeres yderligere."

In English: observations that have been aggregated, blurred or removed in a
table, graph or figure must not be possible to derive by back calculation or by
reading tables against each other. If they can be, aggregate further. In plain
words: no subtracting your way back to a hidden number, within one table or
across tables.

The usual way it happens is a total. Take two rows of a Table 1 with an overall
column:

  | Age   | Overall | Exposed (N = 282) | Unexposed (N = 1,218) |
  | ----- | ------- | ----------------- | --------------------- |
  | 70-89 | 165     | 35                | 130                   |
  | 90+   | 18      | 1                 | 17                    |

Only 1 exposed person is aged 90+, so you hide that number. But the row
still shows 18 overall and 17 unexposed, and 18 - 17 = 1. So you must hide a
second number in the same row, the 17. Now the column gives the 1 back
instead: the exposed column shows N = 282 and every other age group, so the
missing 1 is what is left over. So a number in the same column must go too, and
then one more to close the square:

  | Age   | Overall | Exposed (N = 282) | Unexposed (N = 1,218) |
  | ----- | ------- | ----------------- | --------------------- |
  | 70-89 | 165     | ..                | ..                    |
  | 90+   | 18      | ..                | ..                    |

A reader can still see that the four hidden numbers add up to 165 and 18 across,
and to what is left of each column. But that fits every split from 0 to 18
exposed people aged 90+, so the 1 cannot be found.

The numbers you hide to protect a small one must not be small themselves. If you
hid a 1 and a 3 in the same column, a reader could still see from N that they
add up to 4, and 4 people is a small cell in its own right. Hide numbers so that
the hidden ones in each row and each column add up to at least 5. Here they do:
165 and 18 across, 36 and 147 down.

Usually the better answer is the one DST's rule itself points to: merge
categories ("aggregeres yderligere"). Here a single `70+` group would leave
nothing to hide.

Where to look for numbers that give a hidden one back:

- **Totals, overall columns and N in the header.** Each of them makes a sum that
  one hidden number can be subtracted from. A row or column with a total needs
  either no hidden number or at least two, and the hidden ones together must
  come to at least 5. As the example shows, the second one often pulls in more.
- **Percentages.** A percentage is a number of people in disguise: 0.4% of 282
  is 1 person. If you hide a count, hide its percentage too.
- **The same people in two tables.** If Table 1 shows 18 people aged 90+ and
  Table 2 shows the 17 unexposed among them, the two tables together give the 1
  back. Check every table you take home together, and the ones you took home
  earlier.
- **Subgroups and sensitivity analyses.** If the main analysis has 120 people
  and a sensitivity analysis on almost the same people has 118, a reader knows
  that 2 people are in one and not in the other. When the difference is below
  5, do not give both sizes exactly. One way is to round them, for example to
  the nearest 10; another is to give only the main analysis' size. The same
  goes for the exclusion boxes in a flowchart ([Phase 10 - Build your study
  population](build-study-population.qmd)).
- **The mark you use for a hidden number.** When you hide some numbers and show
  the rest exactly, a mix of marks gives the small one away: if it says `<5` and
  the numbers hidden to protect it say `..`, a reader knows which one is 1 to 4,
  and next to a total that narrows it down, sometimes to a single value. Give
  every hidden number in a table the same neutral mark, such as `..` (a hidden
  17 is not `<5` anyway). Saying in the methods that counts below 5 are hidden
  is fine, since DST's threshold is public.

## Min, max, median and percentiles can point to one person {#min-max-median}

A minimum or a maximum is one person's actual value, and a median or another
percentile is often one too. DST's guidance (PDF above, page 6) allows max, min
and percentiles such as the median only when there is no risk of identifying
individuals:

> "Ingen personer må derfor kunne genkendes i det hjemsendte output."

In English: no person may be recognisable in the output you send home. The
guidance tells you to look
for outliers first and remove them if needed, and for max and min it requires
that the observations at each end of the distribution lie close together, so
that no one stands out. If in doubt, they must not be sent home.

In practice: a median and quartiles of age in a group of several hundred people
are shared by many and point to no one. A maximum income, or the range of a
variable in a small subgroup, can point to one person. Leave min and max out
unless you need them, and ask your data manager when you are unsure.

## Figures and curves {#figures-and-curves}

A figure is judged as if it were the table behind it:

> "For formater, der ikke indeholder tabelceller, såsom figurer eller grafer,
> er en god tommelfingerregel, at de skulle have mindst 3 observationer pr.
> tabelcelle, hvis de blev konverteret til tabeller."

In English: for formats without table cells, such as figures and graphs, a good
rule of thumb is that they would have at least 3 observations per cell if they
were converted to tables. So every bar, point and histogram bin needs the
minimum number of people behind it, and a plot with one mark per person
(a scatterplot of individuals) cannot leave.

DST's guidance (page 7) names three further things to watch:

- **Outliers:** a single extreme point or a long axis can show one person's
  value.
- **Kaplan-Meier curves:** "man fx med Kaplan Meier kurver skal være opmærksom
  på små populationer" (with Kaplan-Meier curves, for example, watch out for
  small populations). Each step in a curve is one or a few events, and the numbers in
  a risk table are table cells.
- **Data stored inside the figure file:** the file must not carry the
  observations the figure was drawn from. The guidance suggests PDF as one way
  to make sure.

How to build figures that meet this is on [Figures](figures.qmd).

## Missing values (NA) are cells too

A count of missing values is a cell like any other. If 1 to 4 people are
missing on a variable, that count may not be repatriated. Merge it into another
category, or hide it the way you hide any other small cell (and check that it
cannot be worked out from the total). Agree the solution with your data manager
if neither fits.

Make a quick overview of missing values, so you see the small cells immediately
instead of adding figures up in your head:

```r
colSums(is.na(df)) # number of NAs per column - spot any 1-4 at a glance
table(df$income_cat, useNA = "always") # one column at a time; shows NA as its own category (otherwise hidden)
```

`table()` hides NA by default; `useNA = "always"` shows the NA row. See
[Phase 7 - `table()` hides NA](inspect-data.qmd).

## How the upload works {#how-it-works}

You upload from the research machine. On its remote desktop there is a shortcut
called "Hjemtag Filer" (retrieve files), which opens the repatriation tool of
DDV App in the browser. There are three steps: upload the files, check them,
then download them to your own computer through DDV App.

- The tool scans each file for possible microdata. The scan is a supplement:
  DST states that it "kan ikke erstatte manuel kontrol" (cannot replace a
  manual check), so the check on this page is still yours to do.
- If a file gets a risk message, you must add a remark saying what the file
  contains. DST's control staff read it.
- Before the files are released you confirm that they follow DST's rules.
- Afterwards DST checks files with a risk message, files over 1 MB, files that
  could not be scanned, and a random 10% of the rest.

Give the files names that say what is in them (`table1_baseline.csv`, not
`output.csv`): it helps the person who checks the file, and it helps you find
it again.

If you are in doubt about a file, DST's instruction is not to take it home
until you have aggregated further or asked. General questions go to
DDVHjemtag@dst.dk, described with made-up numbers, never with real data.

## Checklist before uploading

- [ ] No individual-level data - only aggregated results
- [ ] All cells ≥ 5 observations
- [ ] No hidden number can be worked out from a total, a percentage, another
      table or an earlier export - merge categories, or hide more numbers so
      the hidden ones in each row and column add up to at least 5
- [ ] Hidden numbers share one mark (e.g. `..`), so the small one cannot be
      told apart from those hidden to protect it
- [ ] Min, max, median and percentiles: no outliers, nothing that points to
      one person
- [ ] Figures: every bar, point and bin has at least 5 people behind it; no
      marks for individuals; the file does not carry the underlying data
- [ ] No count of 1-4 missing (NA): merge or hide it
- [ ] Descriptive filenames; no microdata in scripts or logs (no `pnr` values,
      no printed rows)
- [ ] File type is on DST's approved list, with the right extension:
      spreadsheets (xlsx, csv), text (txt), HTML, PDF, Word (docx), code (R,
      SAS, Stata), images (png, jpg, svg, eps and others), presentations (pptx)
